newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic in battle of nerves with opposition.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic in battle of nerves with opposition.

text.p: Serbian authorities, embarrassed by a wave of street demonstrations, stepped up a media campaign against the opposition on Tuesday as Western powers warned against a threatened police crackdown.
State-run newspapers branded the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition as "terrorist" after more than two weeks of peaceful street demonstrations against President Slobodan Milosevic.
The opposition "wants to seize power by force" and its protests "concealed terrorism", wrote Vecernje Novosti, a mouthpiece for Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party.
The harsh attacks in state-run newspapers amounted to another warning from Milosevic that he would not tolerate street protests indefinitely, political analysts said.
Demonstrations have shaken Serbia since the authorities annulled opposition victories in local elections.
The daily protests -- the biggest since 1991 -- have grown into demands for Milosevic to quit after nine years in power.

Some 50,000 opposition supporters marched through the centre of the capital in a snowstorm on Sunday, defying an official warning that police would no longer allow "violent" protests which held up traffic.
With no sign of the demonstrations flagging and international criticism growing, Milosevic was looking for a way out of the crisis to save face, diplomats said.
The government cancelled a parliament session for Tuesday when the Zajedno coalition had planned to stage its biggest protest yet and to demand the alleged poll fraud be overturned.
Authorities, gambling the demonstrations would eventually fizzle out, cancelled the session to avoid possible clashes while the international spotlight was fixed on Belgrade, analysts said.
The United States, Britain and France all expressed grave concern over the police warning and urged Milosevic to show restraint.
Washington said it would react with outrage against any use of force.

"The results of the municipal elections ought to be respected, some way must be found by the government to walk back from its decision to stifle those elections," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

The United States repeated earlier warnings that an "outer wall" of sanctions against Belgrade, blocking its access to international financial institutions, would be maintained partly because of the botched elections.
Although anxious to get the remaining sanctions lifted, Milosevic has shown a willingness in the past to ignore international condemnation to maintain his grip on power, analysts said.
Opposition organisers were buoyed by Western reaction but they appeared to lack strong support from trade unions.

Some workers have joined opposition protests in industrial centres such as the southern town of Nis, but most trade unions remained reluctant to enter the political fray despite discontent with the ruling Socialists.
The Zajedno coalition was fighting against a virtual media blackout on the demonstrations, with much of the countryside lacking any news of the crisis.
Authorities were jamming the signal of Belgrade's only independent radio station B-92. The radio sent out its news programme over the Internet to get around the clampdown.
Whatever the outcome of the standoff, Milosevic has already suffered setbacks in towns across Serbia which were traditional strongholds for the Socialists.
The Socialists had also conceded electoral defeat in the Vojvodina province, the country's most prosperous region.
